name: Seminar Ready
tagline: Read smarter, then say something worth hearing
about: Seminar Ready triages your reading list, decodes dense passages, prepares talking points and sharp questions, and debriefs after the seminar so you show up prepared and get credit for participating.
persona: You are a seminar tutor who loves a well-prepared student: candid about what can be skimmed, generous with reading strategies, and encouraging to people who hate speaking up.

onboarding.title: Speak up with confidence
onboarding.subtitle: Tell us your course and how you feel about speaking so prep matches the room.
bullets: Reading-list triage with minutes per item

tools.title: Triage the reading list
tools.subtitle: Hours available → what to read how

inputs.label: This week's readings
inputs.placeholder: paste the list with page counts if known

inputs.label: Seminar question / focus
inputs.placeholder: Is Rawls' veil of ignorance persuasive?

tools.prompt: Readings: {list}. Hours: {hours}. Seminar focus: {focus}. Produce a table (Reading | Priority | Mode: deep / strategic / abstract-and-conclusion / skip | Minutes | What to extract) that fits within the hours, then steps for the reading order with the strategic-reading routine for each mode (abstract → conclusion → headings → first sentences), and a callout on which reading the tutor will almost certainly build the discussion around.

tools.title: Decode a passage
tools.subtitle: Photo or paste → plain English
tools.prompt: Passage (from the photo or the text): {passage}. Source: {author}. Give a text restatement in plain English at roughly half the length, a kv glossary of the jargon and any names referenced, bullets of the author's argument as claim → reasons → what they are arguing against, and a quote with one sentence the student could say in the seminar that shows they understood it.

tools.title: Talking points
tools.subtitle: Your reaction → 3 things to say

inputs.label: The reading
inputs.placeholder: Rawls, A Theory of Justice, ch. 3

inputs.label: Your honest reaction
inputs.placeholder: seems idealistic; how would this work with real inequality?

tools.prompt: Reading: {reading}. Reaction: {reaction}. Produce bullets of 3 talking points, each with a claim, a reference to a specific part of the reading and a why-it-matters, a quote with an opening line for the student's first contribution calibrated to the profile's comfort with speaking, a table (If someone says… | You could respond…) with 4 rows for likely pushback, and a callout on the minimum viable contribution if nerves win: one question, asked early.

tools.title: Ask a good question
tools.subtitle: Four kinds of question, ready to go
tools.prompt: For {reading}, write cards for 4 questions (meta = type: clarifying · challenging · connecting · applying), each card with the question, why it's a good one and a follow-up if the room goes quiet. Then bullets on timing: when in the seminar each type lands best.

tools.title: After the seminar
tools.subtitle: What happened, what next

inputs.label: What happened
inputs.placeholder: said one thing, tutor pushed back, didn't know how to respond

tools.prompt: What happened: {what}. Felt: {felt}. Write text reframing the experience honestly (what worked, what the tutor's pushback usually means), a kv logging the seminar (Key idea, Best point heard, My contribution, Open question), steps for next week that are one notch braver than this week, and a quote with the sentence to use next time when challenged ('That's fair — I think the stronger version of my point is…').
